title: Life Insurance for Kids: Policy Costs, Cash Value and Coverage Limits
summary: Life insurance for kids is usually a small permanent policy bought by a parent or grandparent or a rider attached to an adult's policy. Here's what to know.
body_markdown:
Life insurance for kids is usually a small permanent policy bought by a parent or grandparent or a rider attached to an adult’s policy. It can help cover final expenses and, in some cases, preserve the child’s ability to buy more coverage later regardless of health. Permanent policies may also build cash value, but that feature can take years to become meaningful. Costs, limits and benefits vary by insurer, so compare current quotes and policy illustrations before buying.


**[A financial advisor can help set up your finances](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sma__falc_relevant&utm_content=lifeinsuranceforkids) so that they are protected and prepared for the unexpected.**


## **Types of Life Insurance for Kids**


A juvenile whole life policy provides permanent coverage as long as required premiums are paid. It also builds cash value.[Guaranteed universal life](https://smartasset.com/insurance/what-is-universal-life-insurance) , or GUL, is another permanent option. It generally focuses more on keeping a[death benefit](https://smartasset.com/insurance/what-is-a-death-benefit) in force than accumulating substantial cash value. Pacific Life’s PL Promise GUL, for example, accepts issue ages beginning at 0.


A child term rider is usually cheaper. It adds temporary coverage for children to a parent’s policy. For example, State Farm currently offers up to $20,000 per covered child, with coverage generally ending at age 25 and an option to convert to permanent insurance.1 The following chart breaks down some of the most common options available:


**Type** **How It Works** **Cash Value?** **How Long It Lasts**


Juvenile whole life Separate permanent policy Yes Potentially life


Guaranteed universal life Permanent coverage with no-lapse guarantee Usually limited Depends on guarantee


[Child term rider](https://smartasset.com/insurance/child-rider-life-insurance) Attached to parent’s policy No Usually through young adulthood


[Guaranteed insurability rider](https://smartasset.com/insurance/guaranteed-insurability-rider) Lets insured buy more coverage later without new medical evidence Not by itself Policy-specific option dates


A guaranteed insurability rider can matter if future health is your biggest concern. Mutual of Omaha’s children’s policy, for example, permits additional purchases without evidence of insurability at specified ages or life events.2


## **What Children’s Life Insurance Costs**


Premiums for children can be relatively low because of their age, but permanent insurance generally costs more than temporary rider coverage for a comparable benefit. Price also depends on the child’s age, death benefit, policy type, state and how premiums are scheduled.


**Coverage** **Sample Death Benefit** **Sample Premium** **Source**


Gerber Grow-Up whole life3 $5,000 $3.70/month Child under 1 in Delaware, March 2026


Globe juvenile whole life4 $10,000 $2.17/month Ages 1-4 in listed states, current schedule


State Farm child term rider $10,000 $50/year (about $4.17/month) Current insurer example


## **How Cash Value Works**


[Whole life policies](https://smartasset.com/life-insurance/whole-life-insurance-quotes) build cash value from premiums after insurance costs and fees. Policyholders may be able to borrow against that value.


Cash value can be small in the early years. NAIC generally advises buyers request a policy illustration, because some policies build value slowly at first and non-guaranteed values can change.


Consider this MassMutual sample illustration for a $100,000 whole life policy. It is for a 21-year-old adult, not a child, so it should only be used to show how premiums and cash value can diverge over time.5


**Year** **Cumulative Premiums** **Guaranteed Cash Value** **Illustrated Total Cash Value***


5 $5,340 ($1,068/year) $2,312 $3,001


10 $10,680 ($1,068/year) $6,768 $8,705


20 $21,360 ($1,068/year) $17,609 $25,942


*The higher illustrated values are assumptions; they depend on non-guaranteed dividends and could be lower or higher in practice.


[Policy loans](https://smartasset.com/insurance/how-to-borrow-against-your-life-insurance-policy) also charge interest. Unpaid loans can reduce the death benefit, and a policy that lapses or is surrendered with loans outstanding can create tax consequences. The IRS generally taxes surrender proceeds to the extent they exceed your investment in the contract.


Overfunding can create another complication. A policy that fails the IRS seven-pay test becomes a modified endowment contract, or MEC. MEC loans and distributions receive less favorable tax treatment, and some taxable distributions can face an additional 10% tax.


## **Coverage Limits and Underwriting Rules**


Juvenile policies usually offer much smaller death benefits than adult policies. Mutual of Omaha, for example, currently offers children’s whole life coverage from $5,000 to $50,000 for issue ages 14 days through 17 years. Its underwriting uses limited health questions and generally does not require a medical exam. Rules can also vary by state.


**Rule** **How It May Work** **Where to Check**


Maximum coverage Insurer may cap juvenile death benefit Insurer


Existing family coverage Coverage may need to be proportionate to family insurance Insurer/state regulator


Health review Simplified questions or additional underwriting Insurer


Consent Parent or guardian may need to approve policy State insurance department


Ownership Adult usually owns policy initially Policy contract


## **When It May Make Sense and the Alternatives**


Children usually do not provide income that a household depends on, so traditional income replacement is rarely the main reason to insure them.


A policy may make more sense when future insurability is important. For instance, a family history of certain health problems could make the option to buy additional insurance later without new medical underwriting more valuable.


Permanent coverage may also fit if you deliberately want to transfer an existing policy to the child as an adult.


If the real goal is saving or investing, compare other accounts first.


**Option** **Main Purpose** **Tax Treatment** **Flexibility**


Child life insurance Insurance / future insurability Cash value has special tax treatment Access depends on contract


[529 plan](https://smartasset.com/investing/529-college-savings-plans) Education Qualified withdrawals generally tax-free Primarily education-focused


[UTMA/UGMA](https://smartasset.com/investing/ugma-vs-utma) General investing for child Investment income may be taxable Broad uses once child controls assets


[Roth IRA](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-a-roth-ira) Retirement Qualified withdrawals generally tax-free Requires earned income


One alternative, a 529 plan, can provide tax-free qualified education withdrawals. Meanwhile, a Roth IRA becomes an option once the child has legitimate earned income. For 2026, the contribution generally cannot exceed the lesser of $7,500 or the child’s taxable compensation.


Before buying insurance on a child, it may also make sense to check whether the adults supporting the household have enough coverage. SmartAsset’s life insurance calculator can help estimate adult coverage needs based on income, debts and family obligations.


Ultimately, though, if your primary goal is building money for college or adulthood, compare the policy’s guaranteed cash values and costs with a 529,[custodial account](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-custodial-account) or Roth IRA before deciding.


## **Bottom Line**


Life insurance for kids can make sense when your main goal is covering final expenses or preserving a child’s ability to buy more coverage later, especially if future health could become a concern. Permanent policies may also build cash value, but that growth can be slow and comes with costs and policy restrictions. If your priority is saving for college or helping a child[build wealth](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/how-to-build-wealth-in-your-20s) , compare the policy with alternatives such as a 529 plan, custodial account or Roth IRA, before deciding.
